newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria chancellor doesn't want new political job.
newsitem.headline: Austria chancellor doesn't want new political job.

text.p: Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky, who announced his resignation on Saturday, said on Sunday he had no interest in any other political job, either at home or abroad.
Vranitsky looked relaxed and cracked jokes at a valedictory news conference as he looked back over almost 11 years in power during some of Europe's most turbulent moments.

Austria's seventh chancellor since 1945 returned to the venue of his first news conference as national leader, Vienna's Concordia press club, to take leave of a press corps caught napping by the timing of his resignation.

"On Tuesday it will be the 10th anniversary of this coalition government. It is an appropriate time to go," the 59-year-old former banker and national basketball player told a packed audience of Austrian and foreign reporters with a shrug of his burly frame.
Vranitzky's resignation confounded political commentators who believed he was in for the long haul after surviving a leadership crisis in October after disastrous European Parliament elections.
Quizzed on his future plans, he said he was looking forward to drinking a glass of fine wine and reading a good book.
He dismissed reports that he had set his sights on a European Union post in Brussels or on the Austrian Presidency.

"I have no interest whatsoever in any political job. I have no ambitions in the international field....and I don't plan joining the big bank," Vranitzky said in reference to last week's takeover of flagship bank Creditanstalt by Bank Austria.
One of Austria's all-time popular politicians, Vranitzky rated his tenure's greatest achievement as guiding an initially reluctant nation into the EU, ending half a century of Cold War isolation.
Austrians voted by a two thirds majority to join the EU in June, 1994. The country joined the bloc on January 1, 1995.

The chancellor, showing signs of wilting in his dark blue three-piece suit from the glare of camera lights, also singled out his programme of economic restructuring, which he said created between 300,000 and 400,000 new jobs.
"During the last 10-odd years we also managed to greatly improve our attitude to Austria's wartime past," he said.
Vranitzky earned respect abroad when he visited Israel in 1993 and said Austria, too, had to account for the horrors committed against Jews by Hitler's Nazi regime.
He counted the national elections in 1994 and European Parliament elections last year as the main setbacks of his political career.

In 1994, Vranitzky's Social Democrats put up their worst performance in a general election, only to be bruised further in last October's European elections when the party won just 60,000 votes more than the far-right Freedom Party of populist Joerg Haider.
Vranitzky said he would not advise his successor, current finance minister and close friend Viktor Klima, on who should become the new finance minister.
"If he makes a decision that turns out badly, it'll be his responsibility, not mine," the grey-haired Vranitzky said with a broad grin.
